title: Encoding performance of cortical neurons critically depends on their morphological and neurophysiological properties
experiments_summary: The study combined computational modeling and electrophysiological experiments in acute brain slices from mouse somatosensory cortex. (1) A simple neuron model (Gauss neuron with soma plus variable-length dendrite) was constructed to assess how dendrite length, background noise correlation time, and population size affect encoding of feedforward input, measured via dynamic gain curves and detection probability using an optimal decoder. (2) Whole-cell patch-clamp recordings (current clamp) were performed on visually identified Layer 4 (L4) spiny stellate cells and Layer 5 (L5) pyramidal neurons in acute coronal and tangential slices from postnatal day 14–24 CD-1 mice. Passive and active membrane properties were characterized using 500 ms current step injections. (3) Dynamic gain measurements were obtained by injecting Ornstein-Uhlenbeck (OU) stochastic currents with embedded sinusoidal components at frequencies of 5–750 Hz into L4 and L5 neurons, driving irregular firing at ~5 Hz. Phase-locking of action potentials (APs) to the sinusoid was quantified via vector strength, and a spike-triggered average (STA)-based dynamic gain method was also applied and validated against the vector strength approach. (4) Background synaptic noise kinetics were measured using voltage-clamp recordings in brain slices with pharmacologically induced network activity via glutamate uncaging (MNI-glutamate) 100–200 μm from the recorded neuron. Intracellular K+ was replaced with Cs+ to maximize space clamp. The autocorrelation of the resulting synaptic current fluctuations was fitted with a single exponential to extract the noise correlation time in L4 and L5 neurons. Spontaneous EPSCs (at −70 mV) and IPSCs (at 0 mV) were also recorded to characterize synaptic kinetics. (5) The effect of background noise correlation time (τ = 2 ms vs. 10 ms) on encoding bandwidth of L4 neurons was tested by injecting OU currents with these two different correlation times and measuring dynamic gain using both vector strength and STA-based methods in 30 L4 neurons. (6) A single artificial EPSC (aEPSC, 20 pA, mimicking a thalamocortical AP) was embedded in slow or fast background noise and injected repeatedly into individual L4 neurons (each sweep treated as an equivalent of a distinct neuron in the population). Peri-stimulus time histograms and detection probability as a function of population size (number of sweeps) were calculated using an optimal decoder with 1 ms and 2 ms time windows to assess thalamocortical input detectability. (7) The role of axonal KV7 potassium channels in encoding was tested by repeating the dynamic gain experiments (with τ = 2 ms and τ = 10 ms) before and after bath application of the specific KV7 blocker XE991 (20 μM). Pre-AP voltage trajectories under the two noise conditions with and without XE991 were compared. All recordings were conducted at 30 ± 2°C using Axoclamp 2B amplifiers, with data filtered at 20 kHz (250 kHz for spike shape analysis), and statistical comparisons used t-tests or Wilcoxon rank tests depending on distribution normality.
